activities.anchor: Fluids are just matter that flows
activities.caption: file each claim under its conservation law — or the frontier
activities.name: fldLawsSort

config.prompt: Two one-line laws and one open problem — file each claim:

items.label: what flows into a pipe must flow out — where the pipe narrows, the fluid speeds up
along a smooth, steady flow, faster movement is paid for by lower pressure
carburettors, atomisers and Venturi meters — a throat literally sucks
why the shower curtain attacks you
chaotic eddies at every scale, mixing ferociously
the wild regime every real high-speed flow eventually enters
one of mathematics' famous open problems

config.why: Two conservation laws, one line each, explain flight and plumbing — what they cannot explain is the subject's live frontier.

activities.anchor: Neck the same flow down to a 2 cm radius
activities.caption: guess the magnitude — the garden hose, quantified
activities.name: fldNeckEst

config.prompt: 10 litres per second flows through a 20 cm-radius pipe. You neck it down to a 2 cm radius. How fast is the water in the neck?
config.why: Area falls as r², so a tenfold squeeze in radius is a hundredfold squeeze in area — and continuity demands a hundredfold speed-up: 0.01/(π × 0.02²) ≈ 8 m/s.
config.context: The wide pipe ambled at 0.08 m/s — a lazy stroll; the neck runs a hundred times faster, with no forces anywhere.

activities.anchor: how fast does water spurt from a hole
activities.caption: which curve is Torricelli's law?
activities.name: fldTorricelliTrace

config.prompt: Water jets from a hole h metres below a tank's surface. Which curve is the jet speed?
config.why: Bernoulli between surface and jet gives v = √(2gh) — identical to free fall from height h. At h = 5 m the jet runs at ≈ 9.9 m/s: pressure head converted entirely into directed motion.

activities.anchor: air must travel further over the curved
activities.caption: true or false — how lift is really made
activities.name: fldLiftJudge

statements.s: Air is obliged to travel a longer path over the curved top, so the flows reunite at the trailing edge — equal transit time.
statements.why: Nothing obliges the flows to reunite — upper-surface air arrives early, and flat plates and upside-down aerofoils fly fine.

statements.s: Newton's view: the wing deflects a large mass of air downward each second, and the air pushes back up.
statements.why: Lift as F = ma on air — one of the two honest, equivalent accounts.

statements.s: The deflection and circulation set up a pressure difference between the surfaces, whose integral is the same lift.
statements.why: Bernoulli's view — the second account; both are correct and measurable.

statements.s: 'Fast air sucks' is the complete explanation of lift.
statements.why: It is only a slogan for the pressure-difference view — the equal-transit-time story bolted onto it is false.

activities.caption: pair each viscosity concept with its work
activities.name: fldViscMatch

config.prompt: One number to rule the flow — pair the pieces:

pairs.right: internal friction — honey runs 10⁴× water; air, surprisingly, only 1/50th of water
fluid in contact with a surface moves with it
the thin region where speed ramps from zero to the free-stream value — where all drag lives
inertia divided by viscosity — a ratio of the flow's two timescales
laminar — orderly layers, momentum exchanged by friction

config.why: Above a few thousand the flow turns turbulent — chaotic eddies at every scale, mixing ferociously.

activities.anchor: The striking fact is how vast the range is
activities.caption: line the swimmers up by Reynolds number
activities.name: fldReOrder

config.prompt: Order these from lowest to highest Reynolds number:
items: A swimming bacterium — Re ≈ 10⁻⁴: inertia irrelevant, water feels like tar, no coasting
Blood in a capillary — Re ≈ 0.001: laminar, cells in single file
A car at highway speed — Re ≈ 4 × 10⁶: turbulent boundary layer (an advantage, as it happens)
A whale — Re ≈ 10⁸: pure inertia, turbulence the default, streamlining everything
config.why: Human engineering spans the same range as life itself — the same water is honey to a micrometre swimmer and nearly ideal to a whale.

activities.caption: guess the magnitude — how fast a cloud falls
activities.name: fldDropEst

config.prompt: A cloud droplet of 10 μm radius sinks through still air. Its terminal speed is roughly…?
config.why: Stokes drag is linear in speed: v ≈ 1 cm/s. Clouds stay aloft because their drops are Stokes-slow — updrafts and turbulence easily hold them.
config.context: By drizzle size (1 mm diameter) Re ≈ 250 and quadratic drag takes over: about 4 m/s; the largest raindrops reach roughly 9 m/s before surface tension shatters them.

activities.caption: drag the divider — smooth ball vs dimpled ball
activities.name: fldDimpleCompare

config.prompt: Same drive, two golf balls — drag to compare their boundary layers:

before.label: smooth — laminar layer
before.text: The boundary layer separates early: a wide, low-pressure wake behind the ball, and pressure drag that costs tens of metres of carry.

after.label: dimpled — tripped turbulent
after.text: The dimples trip the layer turbulent: it costs a little skin friction but pumps fast fluid down to the wall, delaying separation, shrinking the wake — and the ball carries about 30% further.

config.why: At high Reynolds numbers the larger cost is pressure drag, not friction — which is why vortex generators, rough skinsuits and sharks' denticles all exist.
